vignette:
Marilyn, a 71-year-old North American woman, came to treatment after years of keeping her life carefully narrowed around an assault that had happened in the hallway outside her office. She had been working late as a forensic analyst, sorting evidence under fluorescent lights after most of the building had emptied, when a man she had not expected to see forced her against the wall and grabbed her by the arms and torso in a struggle that left her fixated on the most graphic fragments of it: the pressure of his hands on specific body parts, the shock of her own body failing to feel like hers, and the humiliating certainty that she had been overpowered in a place where she had always believed she was safe. In the months and years afterward, what made the memory come back most sharply was talking about it or even hearing the future discussed in ordinary ways, because any mention of plans, retirement, or "what comes next" seemed to pull her straight back into that corridor and into the moment she had most feared. Once Marilyn had come to see herself as inadequate and permanently changed by the assault, even ordinary reminders felt charged; she moved through her days as if they were mined, and that belief made her more likely to scan for danger, avoid conversations, and treat possible triggers as if they were already confirmations of threat.

Marilyn had come to believe that she was inadequate, and that belief settled over the rest of her life with a harsh finality. She used to think of herself as a happy person, but now she described herself as "always miserable," and she spoke about the event as something that had exposed a weakness in her that she could not forgive. If she thought about the assault, she was certain she would not be able to handle it, so she pushed the memory away before she could fully recall it, cutting herself off just as images began to form. Because she believed that speaking about it or staying with the feelings would overwhelm her, Marilyn kept her account brief in session, chose silence whenever the memory pressed close, and used those same habits to keep herself numb in daily life. At times she could summon only a numb outline of what happened, as though it had happened to a stranger, and at other times the fragments erupted with intense rage, especially when she remembered the hands, the body parts he had seized, or the sense of being cornered. Each time those fragments broke through, the thought that followed was sharper and harsher: if this could still come back with such force, then there must be something deeply wrong with her, something that the memory itself seemed to expose. Those moments of partial recall were quickly followed by a hardening of her view of herself: she took the numbness as proof that something was broken in her, and the anger as proof that she was not coping as she should.

As the months went on, Marilyn's sense that she could not tolerate the memory shaped how she lived. Keeping it at a distance also kept it close; the effort of not thinking about it meant she was thinking about it every day, and that same strain made the memory recur with even greater force whenever she finally let her guard down. She avoided exercise, telling herself that if her body became strong or alert it might also become more vulnerable to feeling too much, and she began restricting food in a quiet, private effort to keep herself contained. Three years of avoiding it had given her a painful kind of evidence that she could not cope on her own, and the smaller she made her life, the more convinced she became that she was fragile, inadequate, and no longer the cheerful woman she had once been. Her days at work became organized around safety in the most literal sense: in meetings at the forensic lab she always chose a chair with her back to the wall so she could see the room, scanning for exits and for the kinds of people who might remind her of the assailant. That pattern of protection drew new reminders into her day; every chair she avoided and every route she changed turned the lab itself into a map of the assault, so that the places she would not sit and the people she kept at arm's length became daily acknowledgements of what had happened. She also became uneasy whenever anyone spoke about the future, because those conversations stirred the same helpless feeling she associated with the assault and with the life she feared she had lost. The more she avoided, the smaller her world became, and that shrinking reinforced her conviction that she was inadequate and no longer the cheerful woman she had once been.

The memory itself kept feeding the same cycle. When Marilyn brushed past it unexpectedly-while someone at work mentioned a past case, or when a colleague asked what she planned to do after retirement-she would feel the event rising in pieces, not as a coherent story but as a flash of rage, numbness, and the sensation of being trapped. Those reminders made the hallway and the body-based details feel dangerously close again, which was why future-oriented conversation had become such a potent trigger for her. In response, she retreated further into her habits: she sat rigidly with her back to the wall, skipped exercise, and restricted food when the distress felt unmanageable. Yet those same habits kept the trauma close. Avoiding movement left her more focused on her body, sitting in defensive positions kept the room organized around threat, and eating less left her irritable and depleted, which made it harder for her to feel steady enough to think about what had happened. The more she tried not to remember, the more brittle and fragmented the memory became, and the more the fragments returned as rage and numbness. Each return seemed to confirm her belief that she was inadequate, and each confirmation made the next wave of avoidance feel necessary.

By the time she sought help, Marilyn's marriage and work life had both been affected. She could still function at the forensic lab, but she did so with a tense vigilance that exhausted her, and she had begun turning down social plans because she did not want to explain why she would not sit where others chose or why she went quiet when future plans were discussed. What finally brought her in was the realization that she was no longer just avoiding the assault itself; she was avoiding exercise, avoiding food, avoiding conversations about tomorrow, and avoiding any full memory of what had happened, all while feeling increasingly miserable and unlike herself. She came hoping to find some way to face the memory without being overwhelmed by rage or numbness, and she was most afraid that if she did not, the rest of her life would keep shrinking around the wall she had chosen to sit against.

It shows negative appraisals and avoidance, but not that her negative beliefs cause her maladaptive strategies.
It does not clearly state that her negative appraisals make reminders or triggers more potent or more frequent.
It describes maladaptive strategies like avoidance, but not that these strategies lead to the memory returning.
It shows the memory and later self-criticism, but not that the memory itself generates the negative appraisals in a clear causal way.
It describes avoidance reducing exposure, but not that the maladaptive strategies directly bring back the memory.

It describes safety behaviors and avoidance, but not that these strategies cause additional triggers/reminders.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Memory: The vignette mentions triggers/reminders causing the memory to return, but it does not clearly state that triggers drive the memory in the same paragraph with an explicit causal link.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: It shows negative appraisals and avoidance, but not that her negative beliefs cause her maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: It does not clearly state that her negative appraisals make reminders or triggers more potent or more frequent.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: It describes maladaptive strategies like avoidance, but not that these strategies lead to the memory returning.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: It shows the memory and later self-criticism, but not that the memory itself generates the negative appraisals in a clear causal way.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: It describes avoidance reducing exposure, but not that the maladaptive strategies directly bring back the memory.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: It does not clearly state that her maladaptive strategies produce or intensify negative beliefs about herself.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: It describes safety behaviors and avoidance, but not that these strategies cause additional triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
